notes.hashRouting: jitsi-meet routes rooms by path (/RoomName). The production server answers any non-asset path with the app shell, so path routing survives a root-mounted proxy. It does not survive being mounted under a sub-path.
notes.startup: npm run preview:build runs the install and build stages; npm run preview:start runs the start stage (npm start -> server/index.js), which binds the port from PORT (no flags), refuses to start if the build output is missing, and reports itself ready only once it has served its own request for / (see notes.readiness). Both stages do less than a release build, because a preview runner has fewer minutes and less memory. The install stage runs npm install with MEETSPACE_SKIP_MOBILE=1, so postinstall applies the patches/ overrides and skips the three React Native steps (jetify, android-clean-cmake-cache, android-autolinking); patch-package is never skipped, since the bundles are compiled from the patched sources. The build stage runs npm run build:preview (make preview), not npm run build: it sets MEETSPACE_PREVIEW=1, which builds 6 of the 9 bundles with no source maps (alwaysontop, documentpip and close3 are absent from build/ and libs/), and it sizes the V8 old-space heap to this machine (75% of total memory, capped at 8192 MB, floored at 2048 MB) instead of asking for a fixed 8 GB. Every bundle the served page pulls is built, so the app that starts is the whole app. Demo mode (node demo/start.js, npm run demo) is a separate development path and is not what the preview runs.
notes.externalDependencies: None to build, start or browse. Signalling is only contacted once a room is actually joined, at the backend named by MEETSPACE_BACKEND.
notes.readiness: The readiness check is GET / on the port from PORT; a ready application answers it 200. The start stage announces that state on one line: "[meetspace] STAGE=start STATUS=ready url=http://0.0.0.0:<port>". The line means served, not merely listening: server/index.js writes it only after asking itself for / on loopback and getting a 200 within 5000 ms, which is the same answer a readiness check gets. It is written at most once per run and never alongside a failure, so a run prints either STATUS=ready or STATUS=failed. A start stage stopped before that line ever appeared is reported as a failed start rather than a clean shutdown, because a readiness timeout and a teardown are otherwise identical in the log; a probe that times out against a process that did print it is a probe aimed at the wrong port, host or path.
notes.failureClassification: Both preview commands go through scripts/preview.js. When a stage fails it prints exactly one line of the form "[preview] STAGE=install|build|start STATUS=failed", followed by the command, the exit status (a kill reads as exit=137 signal=SIGKILL, which is what running out of memory during the build looks like) and the last lines of that stage output. Grep the preview log for "[preview] STAGE=" to tell dependency installation, compilation and application startup apart. Stage output itself is streamed through unchanged. The start stage carries a second classification under its own prefix, [meetspace], which server/index.js writes about itself: "[meetspace] STAGE=start STATUS=failed REASON=<token>" followed by the raw failure and one line of what it means. REASON is one of build-output-missing, port-invalid, port-unavailable, readiness-check-failed or internal. The two easiest to confuse are opposites: build-output-missing means the build left nothing to serve and no socket was opened (every missing path is named, with a count, and a zero-byte file or empty directory counts as missing), so it is the build stage failing late; readiness-check-failed means the build output is there and the port is open but the application did not come out over it (the status code or the timeout value is named), so it is the server. README.md, "When the preview does not come up", lists all five.
